claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is governed by the balance between configurational entropy and atomic size mismatch.
The balance between configurational entropy and atomic size mismatch influences whether a single-phase solid solution or a multiphase microstructure forms.
This phase-stability balance is critical for optimizing high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
Systematically varying Al content alters atomic size mismatch.
Systematically varying Al content alters configurational entropy.
Quenching after annealing at 1000°C for 24 hours retains the high-temperature phase equilibria.
Increasing Al content increases atomic size mismatch.
The increased atomic size mismatch destabilizes a single-phase solid solution because its strain-energy penalty outweighs the relative configurational-entropy contribution.
Destabilization of the single-phase solid solution leads to phase segregation.
At low Al content, a single-phase solid solution will be retained after the specified heat treatment.
At higher Al content, multiple phases will form after the specified heat treatment.
Formation of multiple segregated phases reduces phase stability.
An intermediate-Al baseline composition retains a single-phase solid solution after annealing.
The hypothesis is restricted to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys annealed below melting at temperatures that permit sufficient diffusion for phase equilibration.
The exact Al-content threshold for phase segregation is not defined.
The influence of changes in the other alloying elements is not defined.
